influences/basilica-architecture/name: The basilica: Roman civic halls become churches
influences/basilica-architecture/sourceC: The Roman basilica: a large rectangular hall with aisles and an apse, used for law courts, commerce and imperial audiences
influences/basilica-architecture/christi: The aisled basilica church with nave, apse, altar and bishop’s throne (cathedra), the standard form of Western church building
influences/basilica-architecture/evidenc: The derivation of the Christian basilica from Roman secular halls is one of the best-documented borrowings in the history of Christianity. The very name was taken over, Constantine’s first great churches are basilicas, and their plans are closely comparable to forensic and palatine halls. Scholars debate only which secular hall type was the main model, not the borrowing itself.
influences/basilica-architecture/popular: Church buildings are a pagan invention: the first Christians met only in homes, and when Constantine built basilicas he turned the church into a copy of pagan temples (as argued, for example, in Viola and Barna’s Pagan Christianity?, 2008).
influences/basilica-architecture/whatHis: Historians agree that the early church met in houses and then in adapted house churches (domus ecclesiae), such as at Dura-Europos (c. 232–256), and that monumental church architecture began with Constantine after 312. But the model was the civic basilica, not the temple. Roman temples housed a cult statue and sacrifices took place outside at an altar; Christian worship needed a large interior space for an assembly hearing Scripture and sharing the Eucharist, which the basilica provided. Richard Krautheimer emphasised the imperial audience hall as a model, while L. Michael White traced a gradual development from house to hall. The basilica is therefore a borrowing of architectural form for Christian purposes, and Christians deliberately avoided the temple type.
influences/basilica-architecture/summary: From 312 Constantine and his successors housed Christian worship in basilicas, the multi-purpose public halls of Roman cities, giving Western Christianity its characteristic long, aisled church with an apse.
influences/basilica-architecture/story:
The Greek word basilikē (‘royal’ hall) had by the second century BC become the name of a type of Roman public building: a large roofed hall, often divided by colonnades into a central nave and side aisles, lit by clerestory windows, with a raised tribunal, frequently in an apse, from which magistrates presided. The Basilica Ulpia in Trajan’s Forum (dedicated 112) and the Basilica of Maxentius and Constantine (completed c. 313) in Rome were among the grandest. Vitruvius described the type and his own basilica at Fanum (De architectura 5.1), and in the early fourth century Constantine built a vast brick audience hall at Trier, the Aula Palatina.

Before 312 Christians had no such buildings. They met in private houses and, from the third century, in houses remodelled for worship, of which the best preserved is at Dura-Europos on the Euphrates, with an assembly room and a painted baptistery. Some congregations had larger halls by the late third century, since the Great Persecution of 303 began with the destruction of a church at Nicomedia, but there was no monumental Christian architecture. Early apologists such as Minucius Felix even boasted that Christians had ‘no temples and no altars’ (Octavius 32).

Constantine’s patronage changed this. Soon after his victory at the Milvian Bridge (312) he gave the Lateran palace to the bishop of Rome and built beside it the Basilica Constantiniana, now St John Lateran, a five-aisled hall with an apse. Old St Peter’s on the Vatican (begun c. 319–322), the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem (dedicated 335) and the Church of the Nativity at Bethlehem followed. Eusebius’s panegyric on the new cathedral at Tyre (c. 315–317, Ecclesiastical History 10.4) describes its atrium, nave and aisles, raised thrones for the clergy and altar. The bishop’s chair (cathedra) stood where the magistrate had sat in the apse, giving the word ‘cathedral’, and the altar stood before it.

The choice of the basilica was deliberate. Temples were the houses of gods and their images, small interior spaces with public sacrifice outside; Christian worship gathered the whole community inside for readings, preaching and the Eucharist. The basilica was a neutral, prestigious, flexible public building, already associated with imperial authority and justice, and suited to large congregations and processions. Richard Krautheimer stressed the influence of imperial audience halls in which the emperor received homage; others emphasise forensic and commercial basilicas or, like L. Michael White, a gradual evolution from house church to hall. At Aquileia the twin halls built by Bishop Theodore (c. 313–319) show an intermediate stage.

The basilica remained the norm in the Latin West through the Romanesque and Gothic eras, while the Byzantine East developed the domed centralised church and the cross-in-square. Its civic origin has been read in different ways: as a fitting expression of the church’s public role, or as the beginning of a ‘Constantinian’ church of wealth and power. Jerome already complained that churches glittered with marble and gold while Christ starved at the door in the person of the poor (Letter 52.10). Puritans and Quakers later built plain meeting houses, and modern house-church advocates have revived the argument that church buildings are a departure from the New Testament. Historically, the basilica is a clear case of borrowing an architectural form rather than a religious practice.
influences/basilica-architecture/howItHa: Christians had worshipped in houses and adapted house churches, so there was no existing Christian monumental type.
After 312 Constantine funded large churches in Rome, the Holy Land and Constantinople and his architects used the familiar public hall.
The basilica’s nave, aisles and apse suited a large assembly, processions and a presiding bishop.
Christians deliberately avoided the temple form, which was associated with cult statues and sacrifice.
Imperial and civic features, such as the apse tribunal and throne, were adapted for the bishop’s cathedra and the altar.
influences/basilica-architecture/example: Basilica Ulpia, Forum of Trajan, Rome (112): the classic civic basilica.
Aula Palatina, Trier (c. 310): an imperial audience hall, later used as a Protestant church (from 1856).
Dura-Europos house church (c. 232–256): worship before monumental churches.
Basilica Constantiniana (St John Lateran), Rome (begun c. 312).
Old St Peter’s, Rome (begun c. 319–322); Santa Sabina, Rome (c. 422–432), the best-preserved early basilica.
Twin halls of Bishop Theodore at Aquileia (c. 313–319), with their floor mosaics.
influences/basilica-architecture/defende: Praised the new basilica at Tyre as a fitting temple of God and an image of the church (Ecclesiastical History 10.4).
Commissioned the Lateran, St Peter’s, the Holy Sepulchre and other basilicas, instructing bishops to build churches worthy of the empire (Life of Constantine 2.46, 3.31).
influences/basilica-architecture/critics: Complained that churches gleamed with marble and gold while Christ starved at the door in the poor (Letter 52.10).
In Pagan Christianity? (2008) argued that church buildings derive from pagan and Constantinian practice and urged a return to house churches.
influences/basilica-architecture/keptBy/: Catholic churches, where ‘basilica’ is also an honorific title granted by the pope.
Anglican, Lutheran and many other Western churches, whose parish churches descend from the basilican plan.
Eastern Orthodox churches, which used basilicas before developing the domed cross-in-square type.
influences/basilica-architecture/rejecte: Puritans and Congregationalists, who built plain meeting houses rather than ‘churches’ in the medieval form.
Quakers, who reject consecrated buildings in favour of meeting houses.
Modern house-church movements, which regard dedicated church buildings as unnecessary or unbiblical.
influences/roman-law-canon-law/name: Roman law, canon law and church governance
influences/roman-law-canon-law/sourceCul: Roman law: imperial rescripts, codes, the Digest and juristic concepts of person, contract, satisfaction and jurisdiction
influences/roman-law-canon-law/christian: Papal decretals, canon-law collections, Gratian’s Decretum, the Corpus Iuris Canonici, Byzantine nomocanons and modern codes
influences/roman-law-canon-law/evidenceN: The dependence of canon law on Roman law is direct and documented: papal decretals imitated imperial rescripts, the Theodosian and Justinianic codes legislated for the church, and Gratian’s Decretum and the Bologna canonists worked side by side with the rediscovered Digest. The influence of legal ideas on theology (Tertullian, Anselm, forensic justification) is also widely recognised, though its extent is debated.
influences/roman-law-canon-law/popularCl: Church law is just Roman imperial law in clerical dress, and legal thinking turned the gospel into a system of rules and penalties.
influences/roman-law-canon-law/whatHisto: The church inherited Roman law in three ways. First, Christian emperors legislated for it: Constantine recognised the bishop’s court (episcopalis audientia, c. 318), Book 16 of the Theodosian Code (438) gathered laws on religion, and Justinian’s Code and Novels (529–565) regulated clergy, property and orthodoxy. Second, bishops of Rome answered queries with decretals in the form of imperial rescripts, the earliest surviving being Siricius’ letter to Himerius of Tarragona (385). Third, the medieval revival of Roman law at Bologna (from the late eleventh century) shaped Gratian’s Decretum (c. 1140) and the papal law of the next centuries. Harold Berman argued that this ‘Papal Revolution’ created the first modern Western legal system. Whether legal categories distorted theology — Tertullian’s satisfaction, Anselm’s honour and debt, forensic justification — is a theological rather than a historical judgement, and Orthodox writers have often pressed it.
influences/roman-law-canon-law/summary: Church governance in both East and West was built with the tools of Roman law, from the bishop’s courts of Constantine to the codes of canon law in force today. Legal ideas also coloured Western theology.
influences/roman-law-canon-law/story:
The earliest Christian ‘church orders’ — the Didache, the Apostolic Tradition, the Didascalia — were moral and liturgical rule books, not legal codes, and early councils issued short disciplinary canons. Roman law entered as soon as the church became a public institution. Constantine allowed litigants to take civil cases to the bishop, whose judgement was final (c. 318), granted clergy exemptions and let churches receive legacies. The Theodosian Code (438) devoted its sixteenth book to the church, heresy and paganism, and Justinian’s Corpus Iuris Civilis (529–534) and his Novels set rules for ordinations, monasteries and church property, presenting emperor and priesthood in ‘symphony’ (Novel 6).

The bishops of Rome used the forms of imperial administration. Siricius’ reply to Himerius of Tarragona (385) is the first surviving decretal, a letter answering questions with binding force like an imperial rescript. Leo the Great and Gelasius I wrote with the precision of trained Roman officials, and Gregory the Great administered the estates of the Roman church with a civil servant’s skill. Collections of canons followed: the Dionysiana of Dionysius Exiguus (c. 500), the Hispana associated with Isidore of Seville, and the forged Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals (c. 850), which strengthened bishops and the papacy with spurious early papal letters.

Legal thinking shaped theology too. Tertullian, possibly trained in law, gave Latin theology terms such as persona, substantia and satisfactio; Cyprian applied Roman ideas of discipline and penance; the Germanic and Roman idea of compensation for offence lies behind the penitential system and, many argue, Anselm’s satisfaction theory of atonement (Cur Deus homo, 1098). The Reformation doctrine of forensic justification uses the courtroom image of acquittal.

The great turning point came with the Gregorian reform. Gregory VII’s Dictatus papae (1075) claimed for the pope the power to make new laws, and the rediscovery of Justinian’s Digest in Italy fuelled the law school of Bologna. Gratian’s Concordance of Discordant Canons (Decretum, c. 1140) harmonised a millennium of canons with scholastic method; the Liber Extra of Gregory IX (1234) and later collections formed the Corpus Iuris Canonici, the law of the Western church until the Code of Canon Law of 1917, replaced in 1983; the Eastern Catholic Churches received their own code in 1990. In the East, nomocanons combined imperial laws (nomoi) with church canons, culminating in the Greek Pedalion (1800). Canonists shaped European ideas of corporation, representation, marriage law and due process.

Luther burned the books of canon law with the papal bull against him outside Wittenberg on 10 December 1520, but Protestant states soon wrote church ordinances and consistorial law, and the Church of England kept much medieval canon law. Anabaptists and later free churches rejected coercive church law altogether, while Orthodox theologians such as Alexei Khomiakov criticised Western ‘legalism’ as a distortion of the church as communion.
influences/roman-law-canon-law/howItHapp: Christian emperors legislated for the church and recognised episcopal courts (Constantine, the Theodosian Code, Justinian).
Papal decretals adopted the form and authority of imperial rescripts from 385.
Canon collections organised conciliar and papal rulings, including the forged Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals.
The revival of Roman law at Bologna produced Gratian’s Decretum and the classical canon law of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries.
Legal concepts — persona, satisfaction, jurisdiction, forensic acquittal — shaped Western theological language.
influences/roman-law-canon-law/examples/: Constantine’s recognition of the bishop’s court (Theodosian Code 1.27.1, c. 318)
Siricius to Himerius of Tarragona (385), the earliest surviving papal decretal

The Code of Canon Law (1917, 1983) and the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches (1990)
influences/roman-law-canon-law/defenders: Used precise Roman legal language to define papal authority and to rule on discipline across the West.
His Etymologies (Book 5) defined law and canons, and the Hispana collection was later attributed to him.
Built a theology of eternal, natural, divine and human law that integrated Roman and canonical jurisprudence (Summa Theologiae I–II 90–108).
influences/roman-law-canon-law/critics/0: Burned the canon law in 1520 as human law that bound consciences and exalted the papacy.
influences/roman-law-canon-law/critics/1: Rejected coercive church law and the use of the sword in matters of faith (Schleitheim Confession, 1527).
influences/roman-law-canon-law/critics/2: Writers such as Khomiakov argued that juridical categories distorted the church and the doctrine of salvation.
influences/roman-law-canon-law/keptBy/0: Catholic Church (Code of Canon Law 1983; Eastern Catholic code 1990)
influences/roman-law-canon-law/keptBy/1: Eastern Orthodox churches (canons and nomocanons, the Pedalion)
influences/roman-law-canon-law/keptBy/2: Church of England and Anglican provinces (canons and ecclesiastical courts)
influences/roman-law-canon-law/keptBy/3: Lutheran and Reformed church orders and consistories in adapted form
influences/roman-law-canon-law/rejectedB: Anabaptists and Mennonites (rejecting coercive church law)
